notes:
I couldn't finish all three parts. I ran out of searches before I could check the NET Bible notes, Wesley's notes, any Catholic or Orthodox site, or anything on prosperity teaching. I also couldn't read past verse 24 of the Pulpit Commentary or open Matthew Henry's full chapter. So verses 25–29 rest on thinner sources, and parts 2 and 3 are mostly empty. Everything below comes from pages I actually read.

**Overview**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says Zophar writes beautiful poetry and says true things about how the wicked are judged. But he applies the idea so rigidly to Job that he misses the bigger picture and leaves no room for grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/
- Matthew Henry: no teaching was ever "better explained, or worse applied, than this by Zophar, who intended by all this to prove Job a hypocrite." Henry adds that unrepentant sinners don't always suffer this kind of earthly punishment, and that Zophar was wrong there. God's wrath still rests on them, though, as spiritual judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_020.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary calls this speech harsher than Zophar's first, with added coarseness (vv. 7, 15). It reads the whole speech as an indirect accusation that Job is wicked and a hypocrite. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm
- Coffman says Zophar presents what often happens to the wicked as what always happens. He also calls the view purely materialistic, leaving no room for reward or punishment after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-20.html
- Constable says Eliphaz stressed the wicked man's distress and Bildad his trapped position, while Zophar dwells on the wicked losing their wealth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/20-3.html

**v. 1:** Benson says Zophar had nothing new to say. He cuts Job off in a hurry, provoked because Job warned the friends of God's judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-1.htm. Trapp says this is Zophar's last speech in the book. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/job-20.html

**v. 2:** Barnes takes "thoughts" to mean troubled, distracted thinking. Zophar admits his emotions drove the reply, not calm reflection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-2.htm. Gill reads it the other way: Zophar wants it known that his answer was carefully weighed. (same URL). The Pulpit reads "my haste" as a hasty temperament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 3:** The Pulpit thinks Zophar is angered by Job's warning in 19:28–29. It notes that claiming "understanding" sits oddly with the haste he admitted in v. 2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Gill says Zophar felt Job had painted the friends as hard-hearted persecutors and threatened them with "the sword." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-3.htm. Guzik quotes Clarke: Zophar takes back nothing and assumes he cannot be wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/

**v. 4:** Guzik says Zophar claims authority by asserting "we all know this" without proving it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/. The Pulpit says the verse assumes man was created and that a tradition runs from then to Job's day. It sees this as a sign the book is very old. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 5:** The Pulpit calls this a main point of dispute. Job later says the wicked often prosper (21:7, 13), then softens that in 27:13–23. It asks whether rulers like Napoleon really had a "brief" triumph. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Henry says the friends first denied the wicked prosper at all, and Zophar now admits it but insists it won't last. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/20-3.html. Poole says "hypocrite" is aimed at Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-5.htm

**v. 6:** The Pulpit reads this as reaching the height of prosperity and compares Daniel 4:22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Kingcomments says Job may walk with his head in the clouds but will end in disaster. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html

**v. 7:** Guzik quotes Clarke: Zophar hints that he doesn't believe in the bodily resurrection Job had just affirmed (19:25). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/. Kingcomments: dung is swept away and no one wants it back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html. Henry says Zophar means ruin in this life. That is true of unrepentant sinners in the next world, but only sometimes in this one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/20-3.html

**v. 8:** The Pulpit says a dream vanishes when you wake, as in Psalm 73:20. A "vision of the night" is just as fleeting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 9:** The Pulpit says the word for "saw" is rare. It is used of a falcon's gaze in Job 28:7. It compares Psalm 103:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 10:** The Pulpit and Ellicott both say the verb is uncertain. It can also be read "the poor shall oppress his children." The Pulpit prefers "his children seek the poor's favour," either as repayment or because they have no friends left. It adds that the oppressor himself, crushed in spirit, may give the goods back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 11:** The Pulpit and Ellicott say the Hebrew literally means "full of his youth," meaning youthful strength, not "the sin of his youth" as the KJV has it. That strong body still goes to the dust. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Kingcomments: for Zophar, an early death proves that God always punishes the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html

**vv. 12–13:** The Pulpit pictures a glutton holding a pleasant taste in his mouth. It finds it striking that people relish their sins and even boast of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Kingcomments says he keeps the sweet under his tongue so it won't melt too fast. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html

**v. 14:** The Pulpit: in time, failing health or spirits wakes the conscience and the food seems to turn to poison. It cites Bishop Butler. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Guzik says Zophar implies Job's past blessing was the "sweet" that has now turned sour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/

**v. 15:** The Pulpit: fear, remorse, or a court ruling forces the wicked man to give back what he took. Whatever the cause, it is really God's doing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 16:** The Pulpit says these are vague, fierce threats that Zophar knows Job will take personally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. It also notes that the deadly bite of Psalm 140:3 takes the place of the poisoned drink. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-20.html

**v. 17:** The Pulpit calls this the "penalty of loss": missing blessings he would otherwise have had. The rivers of honey and butter are poetic, like the description of Canaan in Exodus 3:8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Kingcomments says honey and curds stand for the highest earthly happiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html

**v. 18:** The Pulpit says he must give up even honest earnings. It gives two readings of the second line: full restitution, or not rejoicing in his gains (the Revised Version, Delitzsch). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 19:** The Pulpit says Zophar is hinting at these charges for the first time. Eliphaz states them openly in 22:5–9, Job denies them in 29:11–17, and the Pulpit calls them groundless slanders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Barnes says this describes taking advantage of the poor, not robbery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-19.htm. Coffman says Zophar piles up charges with no evidence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-20.html

**v. 20:** The Pulpit reads it "because he knew no quietness within." His greed was never satisfied, so he keeps none of the things he enjoyed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 21:** The Pulpit and Ellicott translate "nothing was left that he devoured not; therefore his prosperity shall not endure." The Pulpit links it to Matthew 23:14 and sees a veiled reference to Job's losses in 1:13–19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Poole and Gill offer another reading: he leaves no heir to enjoy his goods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/20-21.htm

**v. 22:** The Pulpit: even while still rich, he will be in trouble, because the poor he made poor turn against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 23:** The Pulpit compares Psalms 78:30–31 and 11:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm. Henry compares judgment striking in the middle of carelessness, as in the flood and Sodom (Luke 17:26). He suggests Zophar may be hinting at Job's children, who died while feasting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_020.cfm

**v. 24:** Ellicott: escape one disaster and another catches him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-20.html. The Pulpit says the word translated "steel" means bronze or copper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/20.htm

**v. 25:** Guzik says Zophar takes Job's complaint about God's arrows (6:4) and turns it against him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/. Ellicott says this is true in general, almost a truism, but completely false as applied to Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-20.html

**v. 26:** Ellicott translates "every kind of disaster is laid up for his secret treasures." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-20.html. Bridgeway: the fire of God's wrath burns them up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/20-3.html

**v. 27:** Trapp says Job had called heaven and earth to witness his innocence (16:19). Zophar replies that all creation has joined against him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/job-20.html. The Pulpit's sermon notes call nature's witness against the sinner the speech's most powerful closing thought. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-20.html

**v. 28:** Guzik says Zophar sees only material loss as judgment. He passes over the loss of fellowship with God, which is what actually horrified Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/

**v. 29:** Morgan, quoted by Guzik: all this was true, but Zophar's narrow outlook made him unjust to Job. Guzik quotes Andersen: the speech never suggests the wicked might repent and be restored. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/. Trapp says even the wicked man's present prosperity is part of his punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/job-20.html. Kingcomments says Zophar ends the same way Bildad did (18:21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-20.html

**Part 2: where Protestant traditions differ**
I found no verse where named traditions clearly disagree. The one real difference in tone is how fair Zophar is:
- Guzik and Matthew Henry say his teaching is mostly true but wrongly applied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_020.cfm
- Coffman refuses to call the speech "eloquent." He calls it "satanic" and Zophar Satan's willing tool. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-20.html

**Part 3: other views**
The only scholarly note I have is secondhand. Guzik quotes an unnamed writer who says to read the poem for its figures of speech, parallel lines and stanza structure, and to appreciate it as fine literature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-20/

To fill the gaps, the next places to look would be the NET Bible notes, Wesley's notes on wesley.nnu.edu, Haydock (Catholic, listed on BibleHub), Gill on verses 26–28, and the rest of the Pulpit and Matthew Henry pages.
